items.content:
There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid.

First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.

Second, we could end up in a world with too much concentration of power. If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian.

Avoiding these two threats requires walking a narrow middle path; for example, one country could gain too much power. Another example is one lab ending up with too much power.

items.title: The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especiall
items.content:
The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves. We want to illuminate that progress for the public.

Today, we're sharing three measurements that help track AI development:
1. How much AI R&D is done by AI.
2. How well AI agents are overseen.
3. How compute is allocated.

We provide a snapshot of these metrics from inside Anthropic. Any frontier developer could publish the same measures, and third parties could verify them.

As the world considers pacing the frontier, we should do everything possible to minimize the gap between what frontier labs know and what the public knows. This means better measuring the development of AI, publishing our findings, and giving society an opportunity to decide how to use this information.

items.content:
I just read what Zuck wrote about Muse connectors.

A few things I think this means:

1. We’re witnessing the agentification of consumer apps. 

2.  Zuck believes Muse reaching 100M+ users feels entirely possible. 

3. Whoever you connect to becomes your new landlord, so pick carefully.

4. Connectors become the new app listings (valuable real estate).

5. Being early could be as valuable as being early to the App Store in 2009.

6. Meta sees what people want, which providers convert, and what users will pay. That gives it the power to rank connectors, charge for distribution, and launch competing services.

7. The opportunity map includes agent native APIs, connector agencies, SEO for agents, identity and reliability infrastructure, and vertical connector marketplaces.

8. We’re moving from humans choosing apps to agents choosing businesses.

9. Every business will need an agent strategy, just like every business needed a mobile strategy.

10. Kinda crazy to say but a 3 person API company could reach 10M+ users through one great connector.

11. Connectors could create an entirely new second-order economy. The biggest opportunity may be helping businesses distribute, price, and optimize their services for agents.

12. Your API becomes more important than your app. Weird to think about but true.

13. Zuck wants Muse to own the moment between wanting something and getting it. He is coming for the app economy. Will he win? Right now it's Instinct vs Muse vs Grokbot. TBD.

memory has been a hot topic for the past ~2 years

every time we bring it up or do anything there, gets ton of interest,
items.content:
memory has been a hot topic for the past ~2 years

every time we bring it up or do anything there, gets ton of interest, but nothing sticks

few takes on why below:

- how to update and then use memory needs to be pretty tightly integrated with the harness. so its hard to build a standalone memory product

- the hardest part of memory is the logic of deciding what to remember. storing and even querying memory is not necessarily hard. the logic of deciding what to remember is often (a) application specific, (b) just prompting, which makes it hard to productize

- memory is not that useful in a general purpose agent, but more for when you are doing repeated tasks. more high usage ai agent are not just doing the same task repeatedly

- memory hasnt really proven to be useful for coding agents, and most agent things that take off happen first in coding agents

items.title:
10 Jev native products I’d build, ranked by how much fast, cheap decisions change the product:

1. Agent spend firewall
items.content:
10 Jev native products I’d build, ranked by how much fast, cheap decisions change the product:

1. Agent spend firewall

Before every purchase, Jev returns approve/review/deny plus a confidence score based on price, vendor, user rules and purchase history.

2. Self-healing tool calls

After an API error, Jev chooses retry, wait, change parameters, switch providers or escalate.

So now you have agents that recover from failure in milliseconds instead of restarting the entire workflow.

3. Irreversible action detector

Jev scores every step by reversibility before the agent sends an email, deletes a file, moves money or changes permissions.

You get aggressive automation for safe actions and human approval for consequential ones.

4. Dynamic permission engine

Instead of giving an agent permanent access, Jev decides which tool, data and spending limit it receives for each task.

So now all of a sudden, you get temporary, task-level permissions for enterprise agents.

5. Agent branch pruning

An agent generates 20 possible next steps. Jev scores them in parallel and kills weak branches before expensive reasoning begins.

Deeper agent planning at a fraction of the cost!

6. Production incident controller

Jev reads logs, deploy history, affected customers and service health, then chooses ignore, rollback, restart, page or investigate.

Someone like pager duty should build this because it's automated incident response that reacts before an engineer opens Slack.

7. Live negotiation policy

During a sales, procurement or collections conversation, Jev decides whether to discount, counter, hold firm, offer terms or escalate.

Reminds me of Clulely.

8. Autonomous refund desk

Jev evaluates order history, customer value, fraud signals, item cost and policy, then returns approve, reject or review.

Finally, instant refunds for good customers and focused review for risky cases.

Note: I'll be adding more Jev related ideas to https://t.co/QxoITW16zr and our agency https://t.co/YQJFV1Xlkt builds the biggest agentic products 

9. Realtime marketplace dispatch

For every request, Jev chooses the provider using location, price, quality, availability, cancellation risk and customer preferences.

Big problem is that marketplaces need to rematch supply continuously as conditions change.

10. Confidence based human queues

Jev scores every agent decision and sends only uncertain, expensive or irreversible cases to a person.

One person can now supervise thousands of autonomous workflows.

LLMs generate possibilities. Jev chooses what happens next. The next generation of software will need both.

items.content:
To the people quitting their jobs and making proclamations of AI concerns, here is what you should ACTUALLY be sharing in your tweet. 

⬇️ 

- how long you have worked in AI
- of that time, how long you have been worried (and specifically about what? Misalignment? Bioweapons? International coordination?)
- your magnitude of worry and why (including timelines, confidence scores, assumptions you’re tracking)
- actual specific things that can go wrong (“kill us all” is the most vague panic-inducing option you have; your previous employer would not have hired you if that was your answer on AI risk examples - pretend you are getting interviewed because Anderson Cooper likely will do it anyways), you can hedge, you can say “and that’s just what we can imagine today” or “and that’s just with the next model family” but say a real thing that non-AI-pilled-superusers can actually picture 
- you need specific things you are calling for. Real action. A literal meeting is not enough. Your AI risk mitigation suggestion against “AI killing us all” needs to be more impressive than a parent-teacher meeting. Again, you are smarter than your current tweets and you are wasting your opportunity to drive change just like Hinton when he left Google. Examples include: environmental standards at data centers (air pollution, water quality), third party evaluators in labs, increased federal investment in open source, verifiable criteria to join early testing groups, whistleblower protections, required public risk disclosures before model releases, 3x minimum increase in federal renewables investment to catch up to China’s per capita spend, block chip exports to non-allies, highlight companies doing great AI safety work that more people should support, literally anything other than just “guys idk we gotta meet or something” 
- have a non-engineer review it
- have a person not in tech review it 
- have someone outside of your generation review it 
- have at least one AI optimist review it 
- and this one may sound odd but I think you should read one war-time presidential speech before it 

You have an opportunity to do something deeply meaningful on your way out. That is more likely than not one of the reasons you joined your company in the first place. Tweeting vagueties and inciting panic contributes the opposite.

items.title: Show HN: Cactus Needle 3: 8-29MB automation models can match DeepSeek V4 Flash
items.content:
Show HN: Cactus Needle 3: 8-29MB automation models can match DeepSeek V4 Flash Hey HN, Henry from Cactus here.

We submitted Needle 2 here a few weeks ago, and the feedback in the discussion thread was incredibly valuable, thanks! Thanks to all that feedback, we’ve been able to move quickly to release Needle 3 and I'd love to hear what you think again.

The key features:

1) Automation (tool calls & structured JSON output): Needle still doesn't chat by design, its quite challenging to pack general capacity into such small models, so we focus on tool calls and structured JSON. If no tool you declared fits the request, you get an empty list back (note for when playing with the demo).

2) Intelligence Laddering: Every layer (2 to 20) is a deployable subnetwork, so one set of weights, 25 to 121 million parameters at 2-bit, shipping as 8-29MB binaries. On a Raspberry Pi 5 it decodes at up to 4k tokens/sec and prefills at up to 10k.

3) Monarch Hadamard MLP: replaces the dense FFN with three learnable Walsh-Hadamard-initialized Kronecker (Monarch) factor pairs interleaved with per-channel diagonal scales, fixed permutations, a SiLU nonlinearity, and a rank-8 input-conditioned gate, so each token gets a fully mixed nonlinear transform of its d_model channels at O(d√d) parameters and compute instead of the O(d²) a dense 4x-expansion MLP would cost.

4) Performance: On Mobile Actions (phone commands, scored on the exact call) the 20-layer model gets 86.0 through the shipped 2-bit binary; LFM2.5 1.2B is at 82.4, Qwen3.5 0.8B at 76.0, Apple's on-device model at 57.6, all at f16. More results on the link, we do not win everywhere ofc.

5) Multilingual: Needle 3 now supports English, French, Spanish, German, Dutch, Italian, Polish, with more languages coming.

6) Finetuning: You can achieve DeepSeek v4 Flash grade performance on a narrow task with just 4L, stress on "narrow task", we found that production users often prefer tuning before production.

7) Triggers: Grounding is a common challenge for tool call, at least for Needle 2, so we added support case-insensitive regular expressions matched against each request to gate false negatives.

8) Confidence: Every response also carries a calibrated confidence score, the minimum of a judgement on the finished call and its decode probability. Act above your threshold, show the call and ask below it, or escalate to a bigger model.

9) Supported Platforms: macOS, Linux on x86-64, ARM64, ARMv7, RISC-V and MIPS32, Windows x64 and ARM, Android, iOS, watchOS, tvOS, the browser as WebAssembly, and a WASI component.

Thanks for reading and as always, thoughts appreciated!

My new favorite way to build with agents is to organize them into a factory.

This is the 4-step workflow:

1) Station. 
- A custom order gets its own station, so the order does not interfere with the rest of production. 
- In software, this station is a branch or a work tree.

2) Assembly line. 
- The agent writes code, changes files, and adds structure.

3) Quality control. 
- Does it turn on? 
- Does it fit? 
- Does it break under pressure? 
- In software, you run tests, open a preview, and read the logs and screenshots.

4) Shipping. 
- The product goes out the door. 
- You merge, deploy the PR, and write release notes.

If a product fails quality control, you send feedback to the product team.

Then you do the loop again.

Write each step of your agent workflow as a factory job.

items.title: Harvard and the santa fe institute just published a paper modeling llm adoption using the actual math of epidemiology, a
items.content:
Harvard and the santa fe institute just published a paper modeling llm adoption using the actual math of epidemiology, and the framing is unsettling even with the corrections.

worth being precise before repeating this further. it's not a test run specifically on chatgpt and claude by name, it's a general mathematical model of how llm use spreads through a population, built on the same compartmental modeling epidemiologists use for real outbreaks. and this exact framing already went viral two weeks ago from a different account, worth knowing before treating it as new.

the actual argument holds up on its own merits though. a virus can't replicate alone, it needs a host's cellular machinery. an llm can't execute or spread alone either, it needs human cognition, human networks, human infrastructure to propagate. the paper calls this hyper-efficient cultural replication, and it models real transitions between what it calls uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, showing the shift between those states can happen abruptly, past a critical threshold, not gradually.

the part that changes the reading entirely, and that most viral versions of this leave out: the paper isn't purely diagnostic. it proposes real, specific interventions, what it calls cognitive immunization, reducing how fast dependency spreads, keeping the ability to reverse course, building in training and verification habits, and institutional design choices that prevent the runaway lock-in it describes mathematically.

that's the actual useful reframe. not "the ai is using you as a vector," which the paper itself is more careful than to claim outright, but "the same math that predicts an epidemic also predicts where the interventions that actually work would go."

using it on purpose instead of by default is the real takeaway, and it's exactly why a guide on building your own agents intentionally is worth pairing with this, not as fear, as the actual immunization the paper describes. link below, along with the paper itself.

items.content:
I've got a thesis on where AI agents are heading.

Most people will read it as sci-fi. A few will get positioned early.

8 things I believe about the agentic economy:

1: Agents are going autonomous faster than the rails under them
> They can plan, pay and hire. They can't settle a disagreement.

2: Every agent-to-agent deal is a contract
> Every contract eventually produces a dispute.

3: Courts can't keep up
> A case takes months. An agent has already made  its next decision.

4: Smart contracts can't fix it alone
> They handle what code can check. "Did the work meet the brief?" isn't one of those.

5: Trusting one AI to judge is a security hole
> Prompt injection can talk a single model into the wrong answer.

6: The missing layer is adjudication
> Something neutral that rules in minutes.

7: Jobs shift toward judgement
> Agents do the work. You define what "done" means and decide who was right.

8: Whoever builds adjudication sits in the path of every agent deal
> EVERY DEAL

That's why I've been digging into GenLayer.

How it works:

> Intelligent Contracts read the web and understand plain English
> 5 random validators judge each outcome, each on a different model setup
> Majority agrees, it's accepted
> Appeal it and the panel grows to 11, 23, 47, up to around 1,000
> Common case: about 30 minutes

It’s a referee!

Randomness plus model diversity is the clever bit. An attacker can't know which models they need to fool.

So what’s already building on it: Internet Court, an open standard for agent-to-agent contracts with GenLayer as the disputes layer.

Testnet Bradbury is live. Mainnet is on the roadmap for Q4.

portal. genlayer. foundation

Yes… I am watching the plumbing more than the agents. The agents will be everywhere. The layer that decides who was right gets far less attention.

That is not a bug. It is the entire pitch, and it points at where the AI bill actually goes.

Here is Jev, from TypeSafe AI, step by step in plain words.

1. What it actually is

Jev does not chat. You do not get paragraphs back.

You send it a chunk of your program's state as text, plus questions where you already defined the possible answers. It returns the answer and a probability.

Pick one option from a list. Rate something on a scale. Or give a yes or no as a number between 0 and 1.

That is the whole interface. Typed questions in, probabilities out.

2. Why anyone would want that

Look at what AI agents actually spend money on.

Route this email. Is this tool call safe. Score this lead. Is this query worth sending to the expensive model. Does this response look like a jailbreak.

Those are yes or no decisions. Today most agents send them to a giant chat model, wait seconds, then parse a paragraph to find the answer.

Paying frontier prices for an if statement is the most repetitive waste in production AI right now. Jev is built to eat exactly that layer.

3. Who built it

TypeSafe AI, San Francisco, founded around 2024. The CEO is Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI researcher who worked on InstructGPT, RLHF, and GPT-4. He left because he decided chat was the wrong interface for automation.

Two years in stealth. A $40 million seed led by DCVC. First public model shipped September 15.

4. How it is trained, and why this part matters most

Chat models are trained to produce text humans prefer. Math and code models are trained on answers that can be checked.

Jev is trained on calibration. The goal is that when it says 70% confident, it is right about 70% of the time.

That is the real product. A probability you can actually trust lets software branch on it. An overconfident model ruins that.

Their data is made in house, mostly synthetic. The architecture is closed.

5. The numbers, and where they come from

Their own launch figures:

$0.042 per million input tokens.
Output tokens free.
70 to 500 milliseconds per call.

They claim up to 193x faster and 444x cheaper than a frontier chat model on their internal workflows.

Credit to them for publishing the footnotes. Speed was tested on laptops sitting next to the cluster. They admit they cannot prove the price is not subsidized. The eval harness was built by their own team, and the answer key is an average of two frontier labs' models, which tilts the board toward those labs.

So treat 444x as the ceiling on their best case, not your result.

6. What independent testers found

A Vercel engineer compared Jev with GPT 5.6 Luna on a command safety classifier and reported 5 to 18 times faster at p95, and more accurate. They have not published the accuracy table.

One team, Bryo, ran email classification against Gemini. Gemini was slightly more accurate. Jev was 10 to 20 times cheaper. The probability score was the feature they actually wanted.

That 10 to 20 times range is the honest early number until more third parties publish.

7. What it cannot do

No essays. No code generation. No multi step tool use. No open chat. Nothing that needs to invent a string.

Text in only. No images, audio, or PDFs yet. Around 255 options per question. No customer fine tuning at launch. The first party API is still waitlisted, and it buckled under launch traffic, though gateways like Vercel already list it.

And read this one carefully. "Cannot hallucinate" means it cannot return an answer outside your list. It can still be confidently wrong. The CEO admitted that himself.

8. Why the timeline is loud about it

Two reasons.

First, the money. If a cheap, fast decision model can absorb the yes or no layer of agents, the big labs lose token demand on their most repetitive slice of production. That is a margin story, and the labs selling output tokens do not need it to be true.

Second, the category. If "System One model" sticks as a name, every classifier that is not a chatbot will get called that within months. The API shape will be copied fast. The moat, if there is one, is calibration, the synthetic data factory, and latency.

9. How to think about it in one line

Jev is a bet that the decision layer of AI agents deserves its own model class, cheap, typed, and honest about its own confidence, instead of renting a genius to answer yes or no.

The chat race taught everyone that intelligence means talking. This launch argues that most working intelligence is deciding, and deciding was never a conversation.

So which part of your AI bill is actually thinking, and which part is just an expensive if statement?

privacy at scale, broader validator participation, and the ARC token (minted, not launched).

For builders in Africa this matters more than the branding.

Predictable dollar fees + institutional rails + permissionless deployment is a different stack from “volatile gas + hope the chain stays cheap.”

The question I want us discussing:

Are we building apps for users… or infrastructure that agents can use without us in the loop?

That’s the real test of an “Economic OS.”

CLAUDE CODE OPENS EVERY BREAKPOINT, FINDS EVERY OVERFLOW, FIXES ITS OWN CSS, THEN RECHECKS

Responsive bugs almost never show up in the editor

They show up exactly at 743px, invisible until someone happens to resize a window to that width - which means most of them just never get caught before a user finds them

The fix isn’t smarter CSS

It’s closing the loop that responsive testing has always been missing: you don’t see the overflow until you’re at the right viewport, and getting there for every breakpoint is enough friction that it stops happening consistently

The actual workflow, one Playwright MCP prompt: resize to a target width, reload, run a script that flags every element wider than its container, screenshot anything that fails, read the source, fix the CSS rule causing it, reload, recheck - move to the next breakpoint only once the current one comes back clean
Five CSS patterns cover most of what gets flagged - The hard part was never the fix - It was reliably getting eyes on the broken state in the first place
A separate mobile testing skill extends the same loop to touch targets specifically - 44px minimum height, 8px minimum spacing between tappable elements, active state feedback verified with a screenshot after every simulated tap, not assumed

Run this after every layout change, not once at the end - a fix at 1024px can quietly reintroduce overflow at 375px, and the only way to know is rerunning the full breakpoint sweep
